screens.title: Large Class & Extract Class
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn to find classes that do too much, understand the risks they introduce, and practice the Extract Class refactoring to cleanly separate responsibilities. A large class — sometimes called a God Object — collects fields and methods for multiple concerns, and that concentration makes the class hard to understand, test, and change safely. You will see concrete symptoms, practical criteria for deciding what to extract, a step-by-step technique for creating new classes, and a live refactoring example in Python. We focus on giving each class a single reason to change, improving cohesion and lowering coupling through composition. As you follow the example, notice how behavior is preserved for callers while the internal structure becomes easier to test and reason about. By the end, you should be able to identify candidate responsibilities, extract cohesive units into managers or helper classes, and run small, safe refactoring steps so tests guide your work. Keep an eye out for two common traps: over-extracting into tiny anemic classes, and exposing too much internal state when moving code out.

screens.title: What is a Large Class (God Object)?
screens.narratorSegment: A large class, often called a God Object, is a class that accumulates many responsibilities, fields, and methods. It typically arises when related and unrelated functionality get added over time without clear boundaries. For example, a class that handles user profile storage, order processing, and notification delivery has multiple reasons to change. The key symptoms are an abundance of fields, dozens of methods that span different domains, and frequent edits for unrelated features. These symptoms make comprehension costly for anyone who reads the code. New team members must scan far more lines to understand the class's purpose. A common misconception is that more features in one place reduce duplication. While that can be true initially, centralizing unrelated behavior produces coupling and a fragile surface where a change in one area risks breaking another. The practical takeaway: treat a class's public responsibilities as the contract you measure cohesion against. If that contract covers multiple domains, it is a candidate for decomposition. Ask yourself: does the class have more than one clear reason to change? If yes, it likely is a large class and needs refactoring.

keyIdea.text: A Large Class bundles multiple responsibilities and often shows many fields and unrelated methods.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is a Large Class?
A class that has accumulated multiple, distinct responsibilities and becomes hard to maintain.
Symptoms
Many methods, many fields, frequent unrelated changes touch the same file.
Why it happens
Feature growth without boundary, convenience additions, or poor upfront design choices.
Common misconception
Putting code together prevents duplication; in practice it increases coupling and makes reuse harder.
Key Takeaway

If a class has more than one reason to change, plan to split responsibilities to improve clarity and testability.

Example: conceptual layout
Profile
Fields: email, address, phone. Methods: update_profile, get_full_address.
Orders
Fields: orders list. Methods: add_order, calculate_total_spent.
Notifications
Fields: notification_settings. Methods: send_welcome_email, enable_email_notifications.
Risk Zones
Testing complexity, tangled change history, reuse blocked by dependencies.
Check your understanding
Ask: does this class have one clear reason to change? If not, it's a candidate for Extract Class.

screens.title: Extract Class — Step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Class is a structured refactoring with clear steps you can follow without breaking behavior. First, identify a cohesive responsibility: cluster related fields and methods that naturally belong together, such as order handling or notification delivery. Second, write or update tests that cover the current behavior of that cluster so you have a safety net. Third, create a new class with a minimal constructor accepting the data it needs; prefer passing explicit values rather than sharing the original class internals. Fourth, move the fields and methods into the new class, keeping method signatures recognizable. Fifth, update the original class to hold an instance of the new class and delegate calls. Sixth, run tests and refactor further to clean interfaces and reduce duplication. A common pitfall is moving code without tests; another is exposing too much internal state. A good rule: move behavior and state together, and ensure the new class has a clear purpose. By performing these steps incrementally and running tests after each small change, you keep the system stable and make the refactor reversible if needed. Extract Class — Step-by-step means identify responsibility, add tests, create new class, move code, delegate, and validate with tests.. In practical terms, a safe, test-first process for decomposing a large class. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactoring Steps
keyIdea.text: Identify responsibility, add tests, create new class, move code, delegate, and validate with tests.

content.html:
Process Flow
Extract Class Steps
1
Identify cohesive responsibilities
Group fields and methods that belong together conceptually, not by convenience.
2
Add or update tests
Cover current behavior of the cluster so you can validate the refactor.
3
Create the new class
Design a minimal interface and pass only needed data via constructor or methods.
4
Move code and delegate
Move related fields and methods, then make the original class hold and delegate to the new instance.
Key Takeaway

Follow small steps with tests at every stage to preserve behavior and reduce risk.

Common Mistakes & Safety Notes
  • Don't move a single stateless method into its own class; prefer a helper function.
  • Avoid exposing the large class's internal state; pass only needed data.
  • Refactor one responsibility at a time and run tests after each move.
  • Look for opportunities to introduce small interfaces to reduce coupling.
Practical example prompt
If a Customer class contains billing and loyalty code, which responsibility would you extract first and why? Use tests to guide the move.

screens.title: Live Example: the Overgrown User class
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the original User class example to see why it is a Large Class. The class mixes user profile fields with order management and notification preferences. This means tests for order behavior must mock or set up unrelated notification state and vice versa. A concrete symptom in the code is the presence of an orders list, notification_settings, and profile fields all in one constructor, with methods operating in distinct domains. Notice the update_profile method directly changes notification state when email changes. That interleaving is a coupling risk. A common misconception when encountering such classes is to keep adding guard clauses and flags instead of extracting responsibilities. keyIdea.title: Spot extraction targets
keyIdea.text: Find clusters of methods and fields that share state — they are prime candidates for extraction.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Original User class
Read the code and identify coherent clusters to extract.
class User:
    def __init__(self, user_id, username, email, address, phone):
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.username = username
        self.email = email
        self.address = address
        self.phone = phone
        self.orders = []  # List of order objects
        self.notification_settings = {'email': True, 'sms': False}

    # User Profile Methods
    def update_profile(self, new_email=None, new_address=None, new_phone=None):
        if new_email: self.email = new_email
        if new_address: self.address = new_address
        if new_phone: self.phone = new_phone
        print(f"User {self.username} profile updated.")

    def get_full_address(self):
        return f"{self.address}, {self.phone}"

    # Order Management Methods
    def add_order(self, order_details):
        self.orders.append(order_details)
        print(f"Order {order_details.order_id} added for {self.username}.")

    def get_order_history(self):
        return self.orders

    def calculate_total_spent(self):
        return sum(order.total_amount for order in self.orders)

    # Notification Methods
    def enable_email_notifications(self):
        self.notification_settings['email'] = True
        print(f"Email notifications enabled for {self.username}.")

    def disable_sms_notifications(self):
        self.notification_settings['sms'] = False
        print(f"SMS notifications disabled for {self.username}.")

    def send_welcome_email(self):
        print(f"Sending welcome email to {self.email}.")
Guided analysis
Cluster: Orders
Fields: orders. Methods: add_order, get_order_history, calculate_total_spent. These share the orders state.
Cluster: Notifications
Fields: notification_settings. Methods: enable_email_notifications, disable_sms_notifications, send_welcome_email.
Cluster: Profile
Fields: email, address, phone. Methods: update_profile, get_full_address.
Example question
Which cluster has both state and multiple behaviors and is therefore the best first extraction target? The orders cluster is a strong candidate because it has an orders list and several methods operating on it.

screens.title: Extracting OrderManager & NotificationManager
screens.narratorSegment: Here we show the refactored code after applying Extract Class to orders and notifications. The refactor creates two new classes, each owning its state and behavior. The User class now composes OrderManager and NotificationManager and delegates calls to them. This preserves external behavior while separating concerns. Notice how constructor arguments give the new classes the minimal data they need: user_id for the OrderManager and user_email plus user_id for the NotificationManager. A useful pattern is to keep simple delegation methods on the original class for convenience while clients start calling the new classes directly over time. Tests become simpler: you can now test order calculations using OrderManager without constructing full user profiles or notification settings. A common mistake is to leave public mutable state that other modules directly mutate; instead, favor methods that encapsulate changes. This refactor increases cohesion and reduces the number of reasons the User class will change. keyIdea.text: Move state+behavior into new classes, update the original to hold instances and delegate to them.

content.html:
Refactored Code
OrderManager & NotificationManager
class Order:
    def __init__(self, order_id, total_amount):
        self.order_id = order_id
        self.total_amount = total_amount

class OrderManager:
    def __init__(self, user_id):
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.orders = []

    def add_order(self, order_details):
        self.orders.append(order_details)
        print(f"Order {order_details.order_id} added for user {self.user_id}.")

    def get_order_history(self):
        return self.orders

    def calculate_total_spent(self):
        return sum(order.total_amount for order in self.orders)

class NotificationManager:
    def __init__(self, user_email, user_id):
        self.user_email = user_email
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.notification_settings = {'email': True, 'sms': False}

    def enable_email_notifications(self):
        self.notification_settings['email'] = True

    def disable_sms_notifications(self):
        self.notification_settings['sms'] = False

    def send_welcome_email(self):
        print(f"Sending welcome email to {self.user_email} for user {self.user_id}.")

class User:
    def __init__(self, user_id, username, email, address, phone):
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.username = username
        self.email = email
        self.address = address
        self.phone = phone
        self.order_manager = OrderManager(user_id)
        self.notification_manager = NotificationManager(email, user_id)

    def update_profile(self, new_email=None, new_address=None, new_phone=None):
        if new_email:
            self.email = new_email
            self.notification_manager.user_email = new_email
What changed and why it matters
  • Orders and notifications now have their own state and behavior, reducing the User class surface.
  • Tests for order totals no longer require setting notification settings or profile updates.
  • Delegation keeps external behavior stable while internal design improves.
Key Takeaway

Extract classes reduce cognitive load and make unit tests more focused and reliable.

Before: Monolith
One class holds many concerns; tests require heavy setup.
Testing
Tests must instantiate full user, set notification settings, add orders, and mock unrelated behavior. This increases fragility.
Change Impact
Small feature changes risk touching unrelated methods and causing regressions.
After: Extracted
Separate manager classes let you test and change concerns independently.
Testing
Test OrderManager in isolation with focused scenarios and fewer mocks. Tests are smaller and more reliable.
Change Impact
Notification changes live in NotificationManager and won't touch order logic, reducing unintended side effects.
Quick check
If a modification to notifications requires changing order methods, coupling remains high — continue refactoring.

screens.title: Design Choices: Composition & Delegation
screens.narratorSegment: Composition is a core principle when applying Extract Class: rather than making the original class inherit behavior, you give it instances that handle specialized responsibilities. Composition clarifies 'has-a' relationships and avoids incorrect 'is-a' semantics that inheritance implies. When delegating, prefer small, explicit methods on the original class for convenience while the bulk of logic lives in the new class. Over time, clients may be moved to call the new class directly. In designing delegates, decide which responsibilities remain the original class's job — often identity and primary domain data — and which belong to collaborators. Also define minimal public interfaces for new classes to reduce coupling. A typical anti-pattern is to let the new class reach back into the original class to pull data; instead, pass needed values through constructors or method parameters. This preserves encapsulation and keeps dependencies one-directional. The practical benefit is clearer boundaries in code reviews and smaller, more focused change sets when features evolve. Design Choices: Composition & Delegation means prefer composition over inheritance and pass minimal data to new classes to preserve encapsulation.. In practical terms, why composition is preferred and how to delegate cleanly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Architecture
Composition & Delegation
Make the original class contain focused collaborators and delegate responsibilities to them.
Design rule
Pass only necessary data to new classes. Avoid letting the new class access private internals directly.
Delegation pattern
Keep convenience methods on the original class while the heavy logic lives in managers. Encourage callers to use new APIs over time.
Misconception
More files equal more complexity. In reality, smaller, cohesive files improve comprehension and reduce review friction.
Key Takeaway

Composition creates clear boundaries; delegation keeps behavior available while improving internal structure.

Practical checklist
  • Does the new class need direct access to private fields? If so, pass the data instead.
  • Does the new class represent a cohesive role with state and behavior?

Example
User has OrderManager. The User updates its email, then forwards that value to NotificationManager instead of letting NotificationManager read User internals.

screens.title: Common Mistakes when Extracting
screens.narratorSegment: Even a correct-seeming Extract Class can introduce problems if done carelessly. One frequent mistake is creating an anemic domain model: extracting nearly all behavior and leaving the original class as a data bag. This can scatter logic and make the original class meaningless. Another mistake is over-extraction: creating many tiny classes each with a single stateless method. That increases indirection without improving cohesion. Breaking encapsulation is a third danger: allowing new classes to freely access the internals of the original object. Instead, pass only the required data into constructors or method parameters. Increased coupling after extraction can also happen when the new classes maintain tight references to each other or to the original class. To avoid these issues, apply a rule of thumb: extract responsibilities that include both state and related behavior, and stop when the new class has a coherent purpose. Run tests after each move and prefer small commits. If unit tests become simpler and fewer mocks are needed, the extraction likely improved the design. A large class — sometimes called a God Object — collects fields and methods for multiple concerns, and that concentration makes the class hard to understand, test, and change safely. You will see concrete symptoms, practical criteria for deciding what to extract, a step-by-step technique for creating new classes, and a live refactoring example in Python. We focus on giving each class a single reason to change, improving cohesion and lowering coupling through composition. As you follow the example, notice how behavior is preserved for callers while the internal structure becomes easier to test and reason about. By the end, you should be able to identify candidate responsibilities, extract cohesive units into managers or helper classes, and run small, safe refactoring steps so tests guide your work. Doing this in small, test-driven steps keeps the system stable. Let's summarize the essential concepts you learned: A Large Class or God Object takes on too many responsibilities, making the code hard to understand, test, and reuse. The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have one reason to change; refactoring restores that principle. Extract Class is the targeted refactoring that moves a cohesive set of fields and methods into a new class and replaces them with delegation, improving cohesion and reducing coupling. Cohesion measures how tightly related the elements of a class are; higher cohesion is desirable. Coupling measures interdependence between modules; lower coupling is desirable. Keep these concepts in mind when you audit classes and when you plan refactorings. Use tests to drive and validate each small extraction so you preserve behavior while improving design.
